t: The battle began by accident when an Allied fleet anchored in the Ottoman base to press an armistice on Ibrahim Pasha, and a clash at the harbour mouth turned into a general engagement.
The Allies had 22 ships to the Ottoman and Egyptian 78, but their ships of the line, heavier guns and trained crews gave them superior firepower; most ships fought at anchor at very close range.

The victory did not end the war: it took a Russian invasion in 1828 and a French force in the Peloponnese before Ottoman forces left Greece, and Codrington was recalled for exceeding his instructions.
dyk: Navarino has been called the last major naval battle in history fought entirely with sailing ships, though most of the ships fought at anchor. After it, some of the bronze from the sunken Ottoman ships was cast into a church bell in Carniola, now in Slovenia.
ev: Greek nationalists revolt against Ottoman rule
Ibrahim Pasha lands in the Peloponnese with 16,000 men and overruns its western part
Britain, France and Russia sign the Treaty of London, demanding an armistice and Greek autonomy
Codrington talks with Ibrahim Pasha off Navarino and extracts a ceasefire until the sultan sends further instructions
The Allied fleets enter Navarino Bay and the battle destroys the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet
Russia declares war on the Ottomans
The Egyptians finally leave the Peloponnese, and French troops clear the remaining Ottoman garrisons by the end of the year
The London Protocol accepts Greek independence

f.place: Navarino Bay (modern Pylos), on the west coast of the Peloponnese, in the Ionian Sea, Greece
f.sides: The Allies (Britain, France and Russia) under Vice-Admiral Sir Edward Codrington, Henri de Rigny and L. van Heiden, with 22 ships and 1,258 guns; the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet under Ibrahim Pasha, with 78 ships and 2,180 guns on Codrington's figures, which exclude smaller boats and fireships
f.outcome: Virtually the entire Ottoman and Egyptian fleet was destroyed, and only eight vessels remained seaworthy; no Allied vessel was sunk.
